questions.stem: What kind of dependency does Fourth Normal Form (4NF) address?
options: Multi-valued dependencies
Partial dependencies
Transitive dependencies
Join dependencies
Domain constraints
questions.explanation: 4NF addresses multi-valued dependencies, where one key determines multiple independent sets of values that are unrelated to each other.

questions.stem: Which conditions must a table meet to be in Fourth Normal Form?
options: It is in 1NF and has no repeating groups
It is in BCNF and does not contain two or more independent multi-valued facts about the same key
It is in 3NF and every determinant is a superkey
It is in 5NF and every fact has explicit time validity
It is in 2NF and has a single-column primary key
questions.explanation: A table is in 4NF if it is already in Boyce–Codd Normal Form and does not store two or more independent multi-valued facts about the same key.

options: A non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute
A column that stores several values separated by commas
One key determining multiple independent sets of values that are unrelated to each other
A composite key with more than two columns
A foreign key that points to two different tables
questions.explanation: A multi-valued dependency occurs when one key determines multiple independent sets of values that are unrelated to each other.

questions.stem: What is the "Cartesian explosion" described in relation to Fourth Normal Form?
options: The growth of a table when repeating groups are split into rows
The duplication of loan amounts across repayment rows
The rapid increase in table count after 6NF decomposition
The creation of false combinations when independent lists are stored in the same table
The failure of a join to reconstruct the original table
questions.explanation: Storing independent lists together makes the relational table combine values across columns even though they are logically independent, producing artificial combinations.

questions.stem: In the loan example, a loan has two collateral types and two guarantors stored in one table. How many rows does the table produce?
options: One
Two
Three
Eight
Four
questions.explanation: The table produces all possible combinations of collateral and guarantors, so two collateral types and two guarantors yield four rows, even if no such paired relationships exist.

questions.stem: How is the loan collateral and guarantor problem resolved under Fourth Normal Form?
options: By creating LoanCollateral (LoanID, CollateralType) and LoanGuarantor (LoanID, GuarantorID) as separate tables
By storing collateral types and guarantors as comma-separated lists
By adding a surrogate key to the combined table
By moving both lists into the Customer table
By making CollateralType part of the primary key of the Loan table
questions.explanation: Each independent multi-valued fact is separated into its own table keyed by the same primary key, so the false combinations disappear.

questions.stem: How does Fourth Normal Form differ in focus from the earlier normal forms?
options: It focuses on atomic values rather than keys
It focuses on how independent lists behave when stored together rather than on how attributes depend on keys
It focuses on time validity of each attribute
It focuses on domain and key constraints only
It focuses on analytical query performance
questions.explanation: Earlier forms focused on functional dependencies between attributes and keys; 4NF extends the discipline to how independent lists behave when stored together.

questions.stem: In which kinds of domains is a failure to recognise multi-valued dependencies most likely to cause subtle data distortions?
options: Domains with a single flat table
Domains with only one-to-one relationships
Domains involving multiple independent classifications, tags, roles or attributes
Domains with no composite keys
Domains that use only surrogate keys
questions.explanation: In complex schemas involving multiple independent classifications, tags, roles or attributes, unrecognised multi-valued dependencies can lead to subtle data distortions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT stated as something Fourth Normal Form provides?
options: Protection against structural inflation
Protection against logical inaccuracies caused by storing independent facts together
Assurance that each table represents one coherent type of relationship
Elimination of redundancy that appears only when projections are re-joined
Avoidance of unintended combinations
questions.explanation: Redundancy that appears only when a table is decomposed into projections and re-joined is the concern of Fifth Normal Form, not 4NF.

questions.stem: Why do many real-world systems implicitly satisfy Fourth Normal Form?
options: Because databases enforce 4NF automatically
Because most systems never use composite keys
Because multi-valued attributes are forbidden in 1NF
Because 4NF is only relevant to data warehouses
Because designers instinctively separate independent relationships
questions.explanation: Many systems satisfy 4NF in practice because designers instinctively separate independent relationships into their own tables.
